title: Diffusion from first principles
snippet: Intuition behind generative models and how we ended up with diffusion
content:
# Data as a probability distribution Look around, you must have seen various breeds of dogs. They're all called dogs, but have differences in features like their size, colour, furriness that make them vary from each other. > In machine learning it is common to realize this diversity of possible images as a probability distribution over the space of images. We call such a distribution a data distribution and denote it as $p_{data}$ ## Statistical Perspective for Real Images Let us consider RGB images with a resolution of 256×256. An image can be represented by a 256×256×3 vector. This means that an image is a point in a 256×256×3-dimensional space. Now, not every pixel combination would correspond to a coherent image. Even when we consider a broad set of dog images, there would only be certain combinations of pixels that make the point represent a dog. Without loss of generality, let us consider the image ${x}$ to now be a point in a ${d}$-dimensional space:\ The data distribution $p_{data}$ can be understood as a probability density function $\mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ that assigns each object $x$ a likelihood $p \sim {data}(x) \ge 0$. ![Butterfly SketchRNN](/blog/diffusion-from-first-principles/pixelspace.png) # Generation as sampling Suppose you are with your friends, and you ask everybody to sketch a butterfly. ![Butterfly SketchRNN](/blog/diffusion-from-first-principles/image-dark.png) You notice something, all the sketches have semblance to what you'd call a butterfly. There is no single correct sketch, unless somebody went ahead and drew a bird that they're calling a butterfly. Everyone has seen a butterfly before; either in photos, cartoons, videos or real life. They vary is wing shapes, colors etc. This represents $p_{data}$. Now creating a sketch ie generating an object ${x}$ can be considered as sampling from the data distribution ${x} \sim p_{data}$. *** # Modelling the data distribution We have established that the real data can be understood as a probability density function that assigns likelihood to images in the dataset. We have also established that generating a new image is modeled as sampling from the data distribution. Thus, if we know the probability density function $p_{data}$, we can directly sample from it to generate new images. ## Modelling $p_{data}$ directly is hard Consider a binary image where each pixel can take values ${0,1}$. For an image of resolution $H \times W$, we would have $d = H \cdot W$, and a total of $2^d$ possible vectors. For a $256 \times 256$ binary image, this gives $d = 65,536$ i.e, $2^{65,536} \approx 10^{19,728}$ possible vectors. Modelling $p_{data}$ directly would require assigning a probability to each of these configurations, which is computationally and memory-wise impossible. Real images are even more complex: a $256 \times 256$ RGB image has $196,608$ interleaved pixels with 256 possible values for each, leading to $256^{196,608} = 2^{1,572,864}$ possible vectors. Besides, only a tiny fraction of these correspond to meaningful images. Thus, in practice $p_{data}$ is extremely complex. It lives in a very high-dimensional space, and assigning exact likelihoods to images is intractable. ## The Basic Idea Instead of modelling $p_{data}(x)$ directly, we map a distribution $p(z)$ to our data distribution. Then, the steps to generate data would look like: 1. Sample a latent variable $z \sim p(z)$ 2. Map it to a data point using a function ${x = f(z)}$
The next question is - how do we find out this mapping function? What does our $p(z)$ look like? We'll train a neural network to learn that! # Autoencoders and VAE (Variational Autoencoder) If we had two sets $A$ and $B$, where: - $A$ is the set of real data points - $B$ is the set of latent points that map to valid data then learning the mapping would be straightforward. We could simply learn a function: $f: B \rightarrow A$ and use it to generate new samples by picking $z \in B$ and computing $x = f(z)$. The problem is we don’t know what $B$ is. So how do we guarantee that a latent is mapped to a data point of the data distribution? ## Autoencoders We learn an encoder that maps data to the latent, and then to ensure a valid mapping, the decoder is trained to reconstruct the input image from the mapped latent. This is called an **autoencoder**. However, this has a drawback from the perspective of generation. Whilst we have successfully learnt the mapping from the latent space to the data distribution, we do not know how $z$ is distributed. Because of this, we cannot sample a new point $z \sim p(z)$. If we can't sample, we can't generate a new image $x$. ## VAE To generate new images, we need to be able to sample from the latent space. A Gaussian distribution is simple and easy to sample from. So if $z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, then we can sample a point from the latent and use the mapping that the decoder has learnt to generate a new image. The math here relies on two tools — [MLE](#/blog/probability-refresher#maximum-likelihood-estimation) and [KL divergence](#/blog/probability-refresher#kl-divergence) — covered in the [probability refresher](#/blog/probability-refresher) if you need a recap. ### Variational Inference #### $p(x)$ as an integral Recollect that our goal was to model $x \sim p_{data}$. For the sake of notation let us write $p_{data} = p_\theta(x)$ where $\theta$ are the parameters that govern the underlying probability density function. Since it was hard to model it directly, we introduced a latent variable $z \sim p(z)$. From probability theory, we can rewrite $p_\theta(x)$ as the sum of marginals $p_\theta(x|z)$ over all $z$. Therefore: $$ p_\theta(x) = \sum_{z} p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z) $$ which becomes, in a continuous case: $$ p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz $$ #### Motivating VAE loss via Maximum Likelihood Estimation In MLE, we aim to find the parameters $\theta$ that maximise the likelihood of the observed data. By doing so, we identify the parameters of the pdf that best explain our data. We define the **likelihood function** as: $$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = p_\theta(x) $$ So the MLE objective becomes: $$ \hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta} \; \mathcal{L}(\theta) $$ Using our latent variable formulation, this can be written as: $$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz $$ In practice, we maximise the **log-likelihood** instead: $$ \hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta} \; \log \mathcal{L}(\theta) $$ So our objective becomes: $$ \log \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \log \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz $$ We cannot directly optimise: $$ \log \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \log \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz $$ To make progress, we introduce a distribution $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ and multiply and divide inside the integral: $$ \log \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \log \int q_\phi(z \mid x)\, \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \, dz $$ Recall that for a continuous random variable: $ \mathbb{E}[f(x)] = \int f(x)\, p(x)\, dz $ Now if we choose $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ as our distribution, we can match the same form: $$ \int q_\phi(z \mid x)\, \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \, dz $$ This is exactly of the form $\int f(x)\, p(x)\, dx$, where: $ f(x) = \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)} $ So we can rewrite it as an expectation: $$ = \log \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \left[ \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \right] $$ Using Jensen’s inequality: $$ \geq \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)} \right] $$ We will now expand the log and rearrange the terms so that it starts looking familiar, and hopefully you can also relate it to the structure of VAE intuitively $$ = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z) - \log \frac{q_\phi(z \mid x)}{p(z)}] $$ Now if you look at the second term, we can rewrite it as the KL divergence between $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ and ${p(z)}$ $$ = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z \mid x) \| p(z)) $$ Now, when I read this, the math is something that can be followed, but I want you to look at the pdfs involved and understand what the represent. ### Making sense of the loss function When training neural nets, we usually seek to minimize the loss function. The loss function is a measure of how far our model prediction is to the true value, the smaller it i #### Prior Distribution In our case, $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ is what the encoder thinks the latent looks like, and $p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ is what we want it to look like. So we minimise this difference.

title: Probability Refresher
snippet: A quick refresher on MLE and KL divergence — the two tools you need to understand VAEs and diffusion models.
content:
The two concepts below come up constantly in generative modelling. This is a quick, self-contained refresher. # Maximum Likelihood Estimation The core idea: given observed data, find the parameter $\theta$ that makes that data most probable. Consider the following [example](https://www.probabilitycourse.com/chapter8/8_2_3_max_likelihood_estimation.php): > I have a bag that contains 3 balls. Each ball is either red or blue, but I have no information in addition to this. Thus, the number of blue balls, call it $\theta$, might be $0, 1, 2,$ or $3$. I am allowed to choose 4 balls at random from the bag with replacement. We define the random variables $X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4$ as: > > $$X_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if the } i\text{th chosen ball is blue} \\ 0 & \text{if the } i\text{th chosen ball is red} \end{cases}$$ > > Note that $X_i$'s are i.i.d. and $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\frac{\theta}{3}\right)$. A Bernoulli random variable models a single binary outcome — it is 1 with probability $p$ and 0 with probability $1-p$. Here, $p = \frac{\theta}{3}$. > > After doing the experiment, we observe $x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 0,\ x_3 = 1,\ x_4 = 1$ — i.e. 3 blue balls and 1 red ball. > > 1. For each possible value of $\theta$, find the probability of the observed sample $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) = (1, 0, 1, 1)$. > 2. For which value of $\theta$ is the probability of the observed sample the largest? Since $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\frac{\theta}{3}\right)$, the PMF of $X_i$ is: $$P_{X_i}(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\theta}{3} & x = 1 \\[6pt] 1 - \dfrac{\theta}{3} & x = 0 \end{cases}$$ Since the $X_i$'s are independent, the joint PMF factors as: $$P_{X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4}(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) = P_{X_1}(x_1)\, P_{X_2}(x_2)\, P_{X_3}(x_3)\, P_{X_4}(x_4)$$ Therefore: $$P_{X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4}(1,0,1,1) = \frac{\theta}{3} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\theta}{3}\right) \cdot \frac{\theta}{3} \cdot \frac{\theta}{3} = \left(\frac{\theta}{3}\right)^3\!\left(1 - \frac{\theta}{3}\right)$$ The joint PMF depends on $\theta$, so we write it as $P(\mathbf{x};\theta)$. Evaluating for each possible $\theta$:
θ P(1,0,1,1; θ)
00
10.0247
20.0988
30
The probability is maximised at $\theta = 2$. For this reason, we choose $\hat{\theta} = 2$ as our estimate — this is the **maximum likelihood estimate (MLE)** of $\theta$. # KL Divergence Imagine you have some prior belief about something, represented as a distribution $q$. You see new data and update your belief to a new distribution $p$. The question is: how much did your belief change? **KL divergence** measures how different one distribution is from another: $$D_{KL}(q(z) \| p(z)) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)} \left[ \log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)} \right]$$ A few properties worth noting: - $D_{KL}(q \| p) \geq 0$ always - $D_{KL}(q \| p) = 0$ if and only if $q = p$ - It is **not symmetric**: $D_{KL}(q \| p) \neq D_{KL}(p \| q)$ in general # Evidence and ELBO The **evidence** is the probability of the observed data under the model: $$ p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz $$ This is also called the **marginal likelihood**, and our original goal (MLE) is: $$ \max_\theta \log p_\theta(x) $$ However, this integral is intractable. So instead, we introduce an approximate posterior $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ and derive a tractable lower bound: $$ \log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}(\theta, \phi) $$ where the **Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)** is: $$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z \mid x) \| p(z)) $$ It is called a *lower bound* because: $$ \log p_\theta(x) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}} + D_{KL}(q_\phi(z \mid x) \| p_\theta(z \mid x)) $$ and KL divergence is always non-negative. In practice, we maximise the ELBO (or equivalently minimise its negative), which serves as a tractable surrogate for maximising the log-likelihood. ### Gaussian Distribution **1D (Univariate Gaussian)**\ $ \mathcal{N}(z \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(z - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) $ **Multivariate Gaussian**\ $ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{z} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{z} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) \right) $ where: - $ \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^d $ - $ \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^d $ is the mean vector - $ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} $ is the covariance matrix # Jensen's Inequality

title: Flash Attention
content:
> Attention was all you needed, but attention needed someone else. There came Tri Dao to the rescue, bringing in flash to help attention. (I suppose I made it too cheesy)


![Flash](/blog/flash-attention/image.png)



 # Background

 ## Memory Hierarchy

Just like a CPU has L1/L2/L3 cache sitting between the processor and RAM, GPUs have a similar hierarchy. From fastest to slowest:

- **Registers / SRAM (shared memory)** — tiny, blazing fast, lives on-chip inside each SM (streaming multiprocessor)
- **HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)** — the GPU's main memory, large but much slower than SRAM

The golden rule: the closer data is to the compute units, the faster the kernel runs.

 ## Forward pass and kernel calls

When you do:

```python
device = torch.device('cuda')
model = LLM().to(device)
```

All model weights — $W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O$, MLP weights, LayerNorm parameters — get loaded into HBM. That's your GPU's "RAM". Every kernel that runs during the forward pass has to pull data from there.

Each kernel follows the same pattern:

> HBM → SRAM → compute → HBM

Load inputs from HBM into fast on-chip SRAM, do the math, write results back to HBM. The next kernel then reads those results from HBM again.

## Why vanilla attention is slow

Self-attention computes:

$$O = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V$$

Let's break down what actually happens on the GPU, step by step:

```python
scores = Q @ K.T          # [N, N] matrix
scores = scores / sqrt(d)
probs  = softmax(scores)
out    = probs @ V
```

Each of these lines is a **separate kernel**. And each kernel follows that read-compute-write pattern. So for a sequence length of $N = 16384$ with float16:

$$N^2 \times 2 \text{ bytes} = 16384^2 \times 2 \approx 512 \text{ MB per head}$$

That's half a gigabyte of attention scores materialised in HBM — and it gets read and written multiple times across the four kernels. As we saw in the [compute vs memory post](#/blog/compute-vs-memory), attention is firmly [memory bound](#/blog/compute-vs-memory): the GPU cores sit waiting while data shuttles back and forth to HBM.

## The fix is obvious (in hindsight)

If the problem is repeated HBM round-trips, the solution is to avoid them — fuse all four steps into a single kernel that keeps the intermediate results in SRAM and never writes them to HBM.

That's exactly what FlashAttention does.

 # Attention!
 Vanilla attention is [memory bound](#/blog/compute-vs-memory). Here's how -\
 Consider a model with context length 16k i.e the input $Q$. $K$, $V$ matrices are of shape $(N, d)$ where N = 16,384. With self-attention being calculated as 
 $O = softmax(\frac{QK^T}{V})V$

title: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA)
content:
> When a I read something, I often like digging down the rabbit hole to find out where it started. What the "original" was. It helps give me a sense of how and why things are; the way they are today. At the time of writing, it has been around 6 months since Yann LeCun together with Randall Balestriero released a new paper titled "LeJEPA".

# Idea
The core idea of JEPA is to address the following thought - \
How could machines **learn** as **efficiently as humans and animals**? How could machines learn to **reason and plan**? How could machines learn representations of percepts and **action plans at multiple levels of abstraction**, enabling them to reason, predict, and plan **at multiple time horizons**?
